common_name: Hopi Orange Watermelon (Drought-Tolerant Native American Heirloom)

planting.note: Sow in warm soil after frost; Hopi Orange is a desert-adapted heirloom traditionally dry-farmed by the Hopi people of northern Arizona using deep planting and wide spacing to capture scarce moisture, and it tolerates heat and drought better than most modern watermelon varieties.

directions: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in warm hills spaced widely apart, thinning to the strongest one or two vines per hill; in dry-farmed desert tradition the seed is planted deeper still, up to 4-6 inches, to reach residual soil moisture, though garden beds with regular irrigation can plant at a normal depth. Hopi Orange is a Native American heirloom watermelon developed by the Hopi people of northern Arizona and preserved through seed banks such as Native Seeds/SEARCH, selected over generations for the ability to produce a crop with minimal supplemental water in arid, sandy soil. Fruit is medium-sized with light green rind and sweet, deep orange flesh that is less common among heirloom watermelons than the standard red. Vines are vigorous and sprawling and still benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set even though the variety tolerates drought once established. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to pale yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — Hopi Orange Watermelon variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Native American Heirloom Watermelons
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Desert-Adapted Crop Varieties

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; unlike most brassica greens, Ethiopian Kale tolerates heat far better and can be sown again in early summer in the Gulf South without bolting as fast as regular kale or collards.

directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 12-18 inches apart, thinning to 6-12 inches for full-sized plants or leaving dense for cut-and-come-again baby greens. Ethiopian Kale, known as gomen in its native highlands, is a vigorous leafy brassica long grown as a staple green across Ethiopia and Eritrea, valued for its notable resistance to flea beetles and other brassica pests as well as its unusual heat tolerance, which lets it keep producing tender leaves through early summer heat that would send most kales and collards straight to bolting. Leaves are broad, slightly savoyed, and blue-green, with a flavor milder than collards but more assertive than standard kale, excellent braised, sauteed, or added to stews. Harvest outer leaves starting around 30 days for baby greens or let the plant mature and harvest the whole head; regular picking of outer leaves encourages continued production from the center. Because it shares pests and diseases with other brassicas, rotate away from beds that recently grew cabbage-family crops.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Ethiopian Kale variety notes

common_name: Aurora Honeyberry (Late-Season University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Aurora is a late-flowering, late-ripening University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred to avoid the spring frosts that can damage the earliest-blooming honeyberries, and needs a compatible late-blooming pollinizer planted nearby.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Aurora is self-infertile. Aurora was released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the leading haskap breeding program in North America, and is valued for its large, elongated berries with a sweet, well-balanced flavor closer to blueberry than the tart, sometimes bitter flavor of earlier haskap introductions. It blooms and ripens later than earlier-generation cultivars like 'Borealis', which helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, and the fruit holds on the bush longer without dropping, extending the harvest window. Like other haskaps, Aurora is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F and flowers that survive down to about -8F, but it is poorly suited to hot, humid climates and performs best in short-season, cold-winter regions. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes

common_name: Borealis Honeyberry (Large-Fruited University of Saskatchewan Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Borealis is one of the most widely planted University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivars, prized for large berry size, and needs a compatible early-blooming pollinizer such as 'Tundra' planted nearby for fruit set.

directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Borealis is self-infertile and needs cross-pollination to set fruit. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, Borealis produces some of the largest berries of any haskap cultivar, with a sweet-tart flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, and ripens in late spring, about two to three weeks before strawberries in most climates, making it one of the earliest fresh fruits of the season. Flowers open very early and tolerate temperatures down to about -8F, but a hard late freeze can still reduce fruit set, so plant in a site that avoids obvious frost pockets. Like other haskaps, Borealis is bred for cold-winter regions and struggles with root and crown health in hot, humid summers, so it is a poor fit for the Gulf Coast and performs best in short-season northern gardens. Minimal pruning is needed for the first four to five years beyond removing dead wood; thereafter remove one or two of the oldest, thickest canes annually to keep the shrub renewing itself.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Haskap Cultivar Release Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
